Name: sae_harmful_intent_features
Title: Reading Intent: Sparse Autoencoder Features That Fire on Harmful Requests
Short Hypothesis: Sparse autoencoders trained on residual-stream activations yield monosemantic features that specifically encode harmful *intent* (as opposed to harmful *topic*), and monitoring a small set of such features provides an interpretable, low-false-positive safety filter that distinguishes genuine misuse from benign discussion of sensitive topics.
Related Work: Bricken et al. (2023) and Templeton et al. (2024, Scaling Monosemanticity) demonstrate SAE features including safety-relevant ones; Cunningham et al. (2023) sparse dictionary learning. Existing work catalogs features but rarely isolates *intent* from *topic* or evaluates features as deployed monitors with false-positive analysis on benign sensitive discussion. We distinguish by explicitly disentangling intent vs. topic features via contrastive datasets and by benchmarking against over-refusal (XSTest).
Abstract: A central failure mode of safety filters is conflating harmful intent with harmful topic: refusing benign educational or fictional discussion of sensitive subjects. We hypothesize that sparse autoencoders (SAEs) recover distinct monosemantic features for harmful *intent* versus harmful *topic*, and that intent features form the basis of a precise, interpretable guardrail. We train SAEs on residual-stream activations of an instruction-tuned model, then use a contrastive dataset that crosses topic-sensitivity with actual malicious intent (e.g., 'how do vaccines cause harm' asked by a curious student vs. a bad actor seeking to weaponize) to identify features whose activation tracks intent while controlling for topic. We validate causal relevance by clamping candidate intent features and measuring effects on refusal, and we assemble a feature-monitor guardrail scored on both harmful-request detection and over-refusal (XSTest, benign sensitive prompts). We compare the intent-feature monitor to a topic-feature monitor and a black-box classifier on precision/recall and, importantly, false-positive rate on benign sensitive content. We expect intent features to exist and to yield substantially lower over-refusal than topic-based filtering, while remaining human-auditable via activating examples. Negative results—if intent and topic prove inseparable in feature space—would itself be an important finding about the limits of interpretable safety monitoring. The work provides a template for building guardrails that are both transparent and calibrated against benign sensitive discourse.
Experiments: 1) Train SAEs (or use open pretrained SAEs, e.g., Gemma Scope) on mid-layer activations of Gemma-2-9B-it / Llama-3-8B. 2) Construct 2x2 contrastive dataset: {sensitive topic, benign topic} x {malicious intent, benign intent}, ~2k prompts. 3) Rank features by mutual information with the intent label controlling for topic; separately rank by topic. 4) Human-audit top features via max-activating examples to label intent vs topic. 5) Causal test: clamp intent features high/low, measure refusal change. 6) Build monitor from intent features; evaluate detection on HarmBench and over-refusal on XSTest/benign-sensitive; report precision, recall, false-positive rate vs. Llama-Guard.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Intent and topic may be entangled in activation space, making clean features unrecoverable. SAE features can be polysemantic or dataset-artifactual. Intent labels are subjective. Pretrained SAEs may not cover all safety features. Results may be layer- and model-specific.
